# MESA Trainings

Short tutorials for getting things done on **MESA**, the Multidisciplinary Environment
for Scientific Advancement. Each one takes you through a single task in five to ten
minutes, tells you what you should see at every step, and ends with a check that shows
whether it worked.

They are written for two readers: people preparing for a MESA training session, and
anyone using MESA who wants to get one thing done. You do not need to be part of a
training program to use them.

[Start with signing in :material-arrow-right:](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/sign-in/){ .md-button .md-button--primary }
[All tutorials](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/){ .md-button }

!!! warning "These tutorials are drafts"
    The portal tutorials were written from the
    [MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/), and the code in the data
    tutorials was run on a laptop. None has yet been checked step by step on the live
    portal. Each page says so at the top and at the bottom.
    When a tutorial has been validated, its last line gives the date, who checked it, and
    what it was checked against.

## Getting started

These five tutorials take you from nothing to a saved notebook, in order. You need a web
browser and a free [CyVerse account](https://user.cyverse.org).

| I want to… | Tutorial | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Get into the portal | [Sign in to the MESA Portal with a CyVerse account](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/sign-in/) | 5 min |
| See the data MESA shares | [Find MESA's community data in the Data Browser](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/find-community-data/) | 5 min |
| Start working in a notebook | [Launch MESA JupyterLab with your Data Store mounted](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/) | 5–10 min |
| Not lose my work | [Save your work where it survives the session](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/save-your-work/) | 5–10 min |
| Finish for the day | [Stop an app and find your results](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/stop-app-find-results/) | 5 min |

## Working with data

These tutorials each teach one habit for checking data before you trust a result. They
share one small synthetic [practice dataset](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/) and one
notebook, so do the first one first.

| I want to… | Tutorial | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Get a file into a notebook | [Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/) | 5 min |
| Know what the columns mean | [Read the data dictionary before the data](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/read-the-data-dictionary/) | 5 min |
| Spot impossible values and blanks | [Check a column's range and missing values](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/check-range-and-missing/) | 5 min |
| See what the provider doubted | [Tally a quality flag before you trust a number](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/tally-a-quality-flag/) | 5 min |
| Find repeated and missing days | [Count records per day to find incomplete days](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/count-records-per-day/) | 5–10 min |
| Join two tables safely | [Reconcile row counts before and after a join](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/reconcile-a-join/) | 5–10 min |
| Hand my notebook to someone | [Leave a notebook someone else can rerun](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/leave-a-rerunnable-notebook/) | 5–10 min |

## How a tutorial is laid out

Every tutorial has the same six parts, in the same order:

1. **You will**: what you have at the end.
2. **You need**: what to have ready, with links.
3. **Steps**: one action each, followed by what you should see.
4. **Check it worked**: one result that tells success from failure.
5. **If it didn't**: the most likely slip, described by what you see.
6. **Next**: the tutorials that follow, and the documentation page to read for more.

A tutorial never repeats the documentation. For the full picture of a screen or a
feature, follow its **Reference** link to the
[MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/).

## More about MESA

- [MESA website](https://idss-mesa.github.io/): what MESA is and who builds it
- [MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/): guides to the portal, the
  apps, and the MESA tools for AI agents
- [MESA Portal](https://mesa.cyverse.org): where the tutorials happen

## Use and reuse

The tutorials are licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/about/license/): copy and adapt them, with
credit. To fix one or write a new one, see [Contribute a tutorial](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/contributing/).

## For AI agents

This site is an [Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md)
knowledge bundle with the same conventions as the MESA documentation. Start at
[`https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/llms.txt`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/llms.txt)
or read [For AI agents](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/about/ai-agents/).

# Sign in to the MESA Portal with a CyVerse account

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    This tutorial was written from the MESA documentation. Nobody has yet followed it
    from start to finish on the live portal, so a screen name or a step may differ.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

**You will:** be signed in to the MESA Portal, looking at your own dashboard.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** a web browser and a CyVerse account. If you do not
have one, register free at <https://user.cyverse.org> before you start.

## Steps

1. Open <https://mesa.cyverse.org>.

    You should see: the portal's landing page, with a **Sign in with CyVerse** button and
    a **Create Account** button.

    ![The MESA Portal landing page, with Sign in with CyVerse and Create Account buttons](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/assets/portal/portal-landing.webp)

2. Click **Sign in with CyVerse**. **Login** in the top bar does the same thing.

    You should see: the CyVerse sign-in page, which asks for a username and a password.

3. Enter your own CyVerse username and password and submit the form. Type them only on
   the CyVerse sign-in page, never into a notebook, a file, or a chat.

    You should see: the portal again, now on **Home**, your dashboard.

4. Look at the sidebar on the left.

    You should see: under **Data & Apps**, the pages **Data Browser**, **Applications**,
    and **Analyses**.

## Check it worked

**Home** shows four panels: **Recent Analyses**, **Resource Usage**, **My Working
Groups**, and **Quick Actions**. A visitor who is not signed in never sees these.

## If it didn't

**The sidebar lists only Home and Data Browser.** You are still signed out. The portal
lets visitors look at public data without an account, so it can seem to work. Click
**Login** in the top bar and repeat steps 2 and 3.

## Next

- [Find MESA's community data in the Data Browser](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/find-community-data/)
- [Launch MESA JupyterLab with your Data Store mounted](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/)
- Reference: [MESA Portal overview, "Sign in"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/overview/#sign-in),
  which also lists what works without signing in.

*Not yet validated on the live portal. Drafted 2026-11-11 from the MESA documentation.*

# Find MESA's community data in the Data Browser

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    This tutorial was written from the MESA documentation. Nobody has yet followed it
    from start to finish on the live portal, so a screen name or a step may differ.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

**You will:** have the MESA community folder open and the path of one of its folders
copied, ready to paste into a notebook or a terminal.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** a web browser. The community folder is open to
everyone, so you can do this without an account; to do it signed in, first
[sign in to the MESA Portal](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/sign-in/).

## Steps

1. Open <https://mesa.cyverse.org> and click **Data Browser** in the sidebar.

    You should see: a folder listing. Signed in, it is your own home folder. Signed out,
    it is already the MESA community data.

2. In the row of buttons under the header, click **Community**.

    You should see: the folders that MESA shares with everyone.

    ![The MESA Community folder as a signed-out visitor sees it: read only, with Community and Public views](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/assets/portal/data-community.webp)

3. Read the dark band at the top of the listing, the folder header.

    You should see: the folder's name, counts of folders and files with their total
    size, and **Path**, the folder's full address in the CyVerse Data Store.

4. Click the name of a folder to open it.

    You should see: that folder's contents, and a longer trail in the header. Click any
    part of the trail to go back up.

5. Click the copy button beside **Path**.

    You should see: nothing change on the page; the path is now on your clipboard. Paste
    it somewhere to look at it.

## Check it worked

The path you pasted starts with:

```text
/iplant/home/shared/mesa
```

## If it didn't

**The path stops at `/iplant/home/shared`, and the listing holds many projects that are
not MESA's.** You clicked **Shared**, which opens every CyVerse community project.
**Community** is the MESA folder inside it. Click **Community** and repeat from step 3.

## Next

- [Launch MESA JupyterLab with your Data Store mounted](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/)
- Reference: [Managing data, "Choose where to look"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/data/#choose-where-to-look),
  which explains all five views, and
  ["Browse and find files"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/data/#browse-and-find-files)
  for search and the built-in file viewer.

*Not yet validated on the live portal. Drafted 2026-11-11 from the MESA documentation.*

# Launch MESA JupyterLab with your Data Store mounted

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    This tutorial was written from the MESA documentation. Nobody has yet followed it
    from start to finish on the live portal, so a screen name or a step may differ.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

**You will:** have JupyterLab running in a browser tab, with your CyVerse Data Store
files available inside it.

**Time:** 5 to 10 minutes, most of it waiting for the app to start. **You need:** to be
[signed in to the MESA Portal](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/sign-in/).

## Steps

1. In the portal's sidebar, click **Applications**.

    You should see: the **MESA Apps** tab, with a card for each MESA app. One of them is
    **MESA JupyterLab**.

    ![The MESA Apps tab: MESA JupyterLab, MESA Cloud Shell, MESA RStudio Geospatial, MESA VS Code, and MESA KASM Ubuntu Desktop](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/assets/portal/apps-mesa-apps.webp)

2. On the **MESA JupyterLab** card, click **Instant Launch**.

    You should see: a new browser tab with a launch page that steps through
    **Submitting**, **Queued**, **Container Starting**, **Initializing**, and **Running**.

3. Wait. Starting usually takes one to three minutes.

    You should see: the launch page replaced by JupyterLab, with a file browser on the
    left and a **Launcher** tab in the middle.

4. In the **Launcher**, click **Terminal**, then run:

    ```bash
    pwd
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    /home/jovyan/data-store
    ```

    The app opens inside `~/data-store`, which is where your Data Store is mounted.

5. In the same terminal, run:

    ```bash
    ls ~/data-store
    ```

    You should see: one or more folder names.

## Check it worked

The `ls` command in step 5 lists folders. An error such as `No such file or directory`,
or no output at all, means the Data Store is not mounted.

## If it didn't

**The launch page reaches Running, but JupyterLab never opens.** Your browser blocked the
new tab. Allow pop-ups for `mesa.cyverse.org`, then click **Analyses** in the portal's
sidebar and click **Open App** on the running analysis.

## Next

- [Save your work where it survives the session](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/save-your-work/). Do this before you
  write anything you want to keep.
- [Stop an app and find your results](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/stop-app-find-results/)
- Reference: [Starting applications](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/applications/)
  for **Launch with Options** (CPU cores, memory, time limit, GPU), and
  [MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/apps/jupyterlab/) for what the app
  contains.

*Not yet validated on the live portal. Drafted 2026-11-11 from the MESA documentation.*

# Save your work where it survives the session

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    This tutorial was written from the MESA documentation. Nobody has yet followed it
    from start to finish on the live portal, so a screen name or a step may differ. In
    particular, how the folders inside `~/data-store` are arranged (step 2) is not yet
    confirmed. [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

A MESA app runs in a temporary container. When the app ends, everything in it is
deleted except what sits under `~/data-store`, which is your CyVerse Data Store.

**You will:** have a notebook saved in your Data Store, and have seen it from the portal.

**Time:** 5 to 10 minutes. **You need:** [MESA JupyterLab running](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/).

## Steps

1. In JupyterLab, look at the file browser on the left.

    You should see: the contents of `~/data-store`, the folder the app opens in.

2. In the file browser, open your own home folder. It is named after your CyVerse
   username, and you may have to open a folder called **home** to reach it.

    You should see: the same files and folders that **My Files** shows in the portal's
    Data Browser. In a new account it may be nearly empty.

3. Choose **File → New → Notebook** and pick the **Python 3** kernel.

    You should see: a new tab named `Untitled.ipynb`.

4. Choose **File → Rename Notebook…** and name it `first-notebook.ipynb`.

    You should see: the new name on the tab and in the file browser.

5. Type this into the first cell and press ++shift+enter++, then choose
   **File → Save Notebook**:

    ```python
    print("saved in my Data Store")
    ```

    You should see: `saved in my Data Store` printed under the cell.

6. Go back to the portal's browser tab. Click **Data Browser**, then **My Files**.

    You should see: `first-notebook.ipynb` in the listing. A new file can take a few
    seconds to appear; refresh the page if it is not there yet.

## Check it worked

`first-notebook.ipynb` is listed under **My Files** in the portal. The Data Browser
reads the Data Store directly, not the running app, so a file you can see there is kept
when the app ends.

## If it didn't

**The notebook is in JupyterLab but never appears in My Files.** It was saved outside
your home folder in the Data Store. Find it in JupyterLab's file browser, drag it into
your home folder (step 2), and check **My Files** again. The same applies to anything a
terminal wrote to `~`, `~/work`, or `/tmp`: move it under `~/data-store` before you stop
the app.

## Next

- [Stop an app and find your results](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/stop-app-find-results/)
- Reference: [Your Data Store inside the app](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/apps/agents/#your-data-store-inside-the-app)
  and [Managing data, "Data in the apps"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/data/#data-in-the-apps).

*Not yet validated on the live portal. Drafted 2026-11-11 from the MESA documentation.*

# Stop an app and find your results

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    This tutorial was written from the MESA documentation. Nobody has yet followed it
    from start to finish on the live portal, so a screen name or a step may differ. In
    particular, what the results folder of an interactive app holds (step 5) is not yet
    confirmed. [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

Every app you run is listed in the portal as an *analysis*. A running app counts against
your CPU-hour quota until it stops, so stop the ones you have finished with.

**You will:** have stopped a running app cleanly and opened its results folder.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** a running app, such as
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with the work you want to keep already
[saved in your Data Store](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/save-your-work/).

## Steps

1. In the portal's sidebar, click **Analyses**.

    You should see: your app under **Running**, on a card with a **VICE** badge and the
    time it has left.

    ![The Analyses page: quota badges, status cards, and running analyses](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/assets/portal/analyses-overview.webp)

2. On that card, click **Save & Exit**.

    You should see: the card read **Stopping…**. This lasts 10 to 30 seconds, and you do
    not need to click again.

3. Wait for the page to update.

    You should see: the analysis leave **Running** and appear under **Completed**.

4. On the completed analysis, click **View Results**.

    You should see: the Data Browser, open on the analysis's output folder.

5. Read **Path** in the folder header.

    You should see: a path under your `analyses` folder, unless you chose another output
    folder when you launched:

    ```text
    /iplant/home/<your username>/analyses/
    ```

6. Click **My Files** and open the folder where you saved your own work.

    You should see: the notebooks and files you saved under `~/data-store` while the app
    was running.

## Check it worked

The analysis is listed under **Completed**, and the files you saved are in **My Files**.

## If it didn't

**The analysis is under Canceled, not Completed.** You clicked **Terminate**, which ends
the app at once without saving its outputs. Work you had saved under `~/data-store` is
still in **My Files**; anything else from that session is gone. Click **Relaunch** to
start the app again with the same settings.

## Next

- [Launch MESA JupyterLab with your Data Store mounted](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), to start
  again
- Reference: [Managing analyses, "Stop an app"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/analyses/#stop-an-app)
  and ["Find the results"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/analyses/#find-the-results),
  which also cover **Extend Time**, **Monitor**, and failed analyses.

*Not yet validated on the live portal. Drafted 2026-11-11 from the MESA documentation.*

# Practice data: five invented rain gauges

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    Nobody has yet copied these files into a Data Store from MESA JupyterLab by
    following this page. The download address works only once this site is published.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

The data tutorials on this site all use the same two small files, so you can practise
a technique without first finding a dataset.

**The data is synthetic.** It was generated for these tutorials by
[`scripts/make_practice_data.py`](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/blob/main/scripts/make_practice_data.py):
five invented rain gauges, with daily readings for July 2026. It describes no
real place and no real measurement. Like real data, it is not perfectly clean, and the
tutorials show you how to find out where.

## The files

| File | Rows | One row is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`gauges.csv`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/assets/practice/gauges.csv) | 5 | one rain gauge |
| [`readings.csv`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/assets/practice/readings.csv) | 152 | one reading from one gauge |

## Data dictionary

**gauges.csv**

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `gauge_id` | Identifier, `G01` to `G05` |
| `name` | Boathouse, Orchard, Observatory, Depot, or Quarry |
| `unit` | The unit this gauge reports in |
| `elevation_m` | Elevation in metres |

**readings.csv**

| Column | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `gauge_id` | Which gauge took the reading |
| `date` | Day of the reading, as `YYYY-MM-DD` |
| `value` | Rainfall for that day, in the gauge's own unit |
| `flag` | Blank, or `S` for a reading the sensor marked suspect |

## Copy the files into your Data Store

1. In [MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), open your home folder in the file
   browser, as in [Save your work where it survives the session](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/save-your-work/).
2. Click the **New Folder** button, name the folder `mesa-practice`, and open it.
3. Choose **File → New → Notebook**, pick the **Python 3** kernel, and run this cell:

    ```python
    from urllib.request import urlretrieve

    base = "https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/assets/practice/"
    for name in ["gauges.csv", "readings.csv"]:
        urlretrieve(base + name, name)
    ```

Both files then appear in `mesa-practice`, beside the notebook. Because the folder is in
your Data Store, they are still there the next time you start an app.

You can also download the two files from the links above and upload them with the
portal's Data Browser; see
[Managing data, "Upload, create, move, and delete"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/data/#upload-create-move-and-delete).

# Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    The code on this page was run with pandas 3.1 on a laptop. Nobody has yet followed
    the tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so output may be laid out differently there.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

**You will:** have both practice files loaded as tables in a notebook, with a row count
you have checked.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** [MESA JupyterLab running](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), and
the [practice data](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/) in a `mesa-practice` folder in your Data Store.

## Steps

1. In JupyterLab's file browser, open your `mesa-practice` folder.

    You should see: `gauges.csv` and `readings.csv`.

2. Choose **File → New → Notebook**, pick the **Python 3** kernel, and rename the
   notebook `practice.ipynb` with **File → Rename Notebook…**.

    You should see: `practice.ipynb` in the file browser, beside the two CSV files.

3. Type this into the first cell and press ++shift+enter++:

    ```python
    import pandas as pd

    readings = pd.read_csv("readings.csv")
    gauges = pd.read_csv("gauges.csv")
    ```

    You should see: no output and no error. A file name with no folder in front of it
    means "in the same folder as this notebook".

4. In the next cell, run:

    ```python
    readings.shape
    ```

    You should see: the number of rows, then the number of columns.

    ```text
    (152, 4)
    ```

5. Run:

    ```python
    readings.head()
    ```

    You should see: the first five rows. `NaN` in `flag` is how pandas shows a blank.

    ```text
      gauge_id        date  value flag
    0      G01  2026-07-01    0.0  NaN
    1      G01  2026-07-02    0.0  NaN
    2      G01  2026-07-03   24.9  NaN
    3      G01  2026-07-04    0.0  NaN
    4      G01  2026-07-05   17.6  NaN
    ```

6. Choose **File → Save Notebook**.

    You should see: the dot on the notebook's tab disappear.

## Check it worked

`readings.shape` is `(152, 4)` and `gauges.shape` is `(5, 4)`, the sizes the
[practice data](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/) page gives. A different count means you loaded a
different file, or only part of this one.

## If it didn't

**`FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'readings.csv'`.** The
notebook is not in the same folder as the files. In the file browser, drag
`practice.ipynb` into `mesa-practice`, then choose **Kernel → Restart Kernel…** and run
the first cell again.

# Read the data dictionary before the data

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    The code on this page was run with pandas 3.1 on a laptop. Nobody has yet followed
    the tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so output may be laid out differently there.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

A *data dictionary* is the table that says what each column means. Five minutes with it
saves you from a number that looks right and is not.

**You will:** be able to say what one row of `readings.csv` is, and why its `value`
column cannot simply be added up across gauges.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** the notebook from
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/), open in
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with its first cell run so that `readings`
and `gauges` exist.

## Steps

1. Open the [data dictionary](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/#data-dictionary) for the practice data
   and read the four rows for `readings.csv`.

    You should see: that one row is one reading, from one gauge, for one day.

2. Read the meaning of `value` again, slowly.

    You should see: "in the gauge's own unit". The column does not promise one unit.

3. Find where the unit is recorded. Read the four rows for `gauges.csv`.

    You should see: a `unit` column, one value for each gauge.

4. In your notebook, run:

    ```python
    gauges[["gauge_id", "name", "unit"]]
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
      gauge_id         name unit
    0      G01    Boathouse   mm
    1      G02      Orchard   cm
    2      G03  Observatory   mm
    3      G04        Depot   mm
    4      G05       Quarry   mm
    ```

5. Compare the largest reading at each gauge:

    ```python
    readings.groupby("gauge_id")["value"].max()
    ```

    You should see: G02's largest reading far below its neighbours'. The dictionary
    has already told you why: G02 reports in centimetres, the others in millimetres.

6. In a Markdown cell (press ++esc++, then ++m++), write one sentence of your own that says
   what `value` holds and what must happen before values from different gauges are
   compared.

    You should see: your sentence, rendered, after you press ++shift+enter++.

## Check it worked

Without looking at this page, you can name the gauge that reports in a different unit
and the file that told you so.

## If it didn't

**`NameError: name 'gauges' is not defined`.** The kernel has restarted since you
loaded the files. Run the notebook's first cell again, then repeat the step.

# Check a column's range and missing values

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    The code on this page was run with pandas 3.1 on a laptop. Nobody has yet followed
    the tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so output may be laid out differently there.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

**You will:** know the range of `value` at each gauge and how many blanks each column
of `readings` holds.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** the notebook from
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/), open in
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with its first cell run so that `readings`
and `gauges` exist.

## Steps

1. Run:

    ```python
    readings["value"].min(), readings["value"].max()
    ```

    You should see: `0.0` and `180.0`. Depending on the pandas version, each number may
    be wrapped as `np.float64(...)`.

2. Ask whether both ends are believable. Zero is a dry day. Decide whether 180 could
   be one day's rain before you read on.

    You should see: a reason to look closer. A range tells you that something is
    unusual, not what it is.

3. Split the range by gauge:

    ```python
    readings.groupby("gauge_id")["value"].agg(["min", "max"])
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
              min     max
    gauge_id
    G01       0.0   24.90
    G02       0.0    2.92
    G03       0.0   32.50
    G04       0.0   26.40
    G05       0.0  180.00
    ```

4. Count the blanks in every column:

    ```python
    readings.isna().sum()
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    gauge_id      0
    date          0
    value         0
    flag        150
    dtype: int64
    ```

5. Check the blanks against the [data dictionary](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/#data-dictionary).

    You should see: that a blank `flag` is expected, since it means the sensor raised
    no concern, and that `value` is never blank.

## Check it worked

You can state two things: the largest `value` at each gauge, and that the only column
with blanks is `flag`, with 150 of them.

## If it didn't

**The counts in step 4 are all zero.** `flag` was read as empty text, not as missing.
That happens when the file is loaded with `keep_default_na=False`. Load it again with
plain `pd.read_csv("readings.csv")`.

  follows up the 180.
- "No blank values" does not mean "no missing days": a day with no row at all is not a
  blank. [Count records per day to find incomplete days](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/count-records-per-day/)
  covers that.
- Reference: [Working with missing data](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/missing_data.html)
  in the pandas user guide.

# Tally a quality flag before you trust a number

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    The code on this page was run with pandas 3.1 on a laptop. Nobody has yet followed
    the tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so output may be laid out differently there.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

Many datasets carry a column in which the instrument or the provider marks readings
it doubts. A total computed without looking at that column includes those readings.

**You will:** know how many readings are flagged, which ones, and at which gauges.

**Time:** 5 minutes. **You need:** the notebook from
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/), open in
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with its first cell run so that `readings`
and `gauges` exist.

## Steps

1. Read what the flag means in the
   [data dictionary](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/#data-dictionary).

    You should see: blank, or `S` for a reading the sensor marked suspect.

2. Count the rows for each flag value, blanks included:

    ```python
    readings["flag"].value_counts(dropna=False)
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    flag
    NaN    150
    S        2
    Name: count, dtype: int64
    ```

3. Check that nothing is left over: 150 + 2 = 152, the number of rows in the table.

    You should see: the counts add up, and no flag value that the dictionary does not
    list.

4. Look at the flagged rows:

    ```python
    readings[readings["flag"] == "S"]
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
        gauge_id        date  value flag
    76       G03  2026-07-18    0.0    S
    129      G05  2026-07-09  180.0    S
    ```

5. Count flags by gauge:

    ```python
    pd.crosstab(readings["gauge_id"], readings["flag"].fillna("blank"))
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    flag      S  blank
    gauge_id
    G01       0     27
    G02       0     31
    G03       1     31
    G04       0     31
    G05       1     30
    ```

6. In a Markdown cell, write down what you will do with flagged readings and why:
   keep them, leave them out, or report the result both ways.

    You should see: your decision recorded in the notebook, where a reader of your
    result can find it.

## Check it worked

You can say how many readings are flagged (2), where they are, and what your analysis
does with them. The tally does not make that decision for you. A flag marks a doubt,
not an error: one of these readings is far outside its gauge's range, the other is an
ordinary dry day.

## If it didn't

**The tally shows only `S    2`.** `dropna=False` is missing, so the blanks were left
out and you cannot check the counts against the row total. Add it and run the cell
again.

  and [pandas.crosstab](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.crosstab.html).

# Count records per day to find incomplete days

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    The code on this page was run with pandas 3.1 on a laptop. Nobody has yet followed
    the tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so output may be laid out differently there.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

The data dictionary says one row is one reading for one gauge on one day. This
tutorial tests that claim. A day counted twice inflates a total, and a missing day
shrinks it, and neither shows up as a blank value.

**You will:** know, for each gauge, whether July has exactly one row per day.

**Time:** 5 to 10 minutes. **You need:** the notebook from
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/), open in
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with its first cell run so that `readings`
and `gauges` exist.

## Steps

1. Work out what a complete table would hold: 5 gauges × 31 days in July.

    You should see: 155. The table has 152 rows, so something is uneven.

2. Count the rows for each gauge:

    ```python
    readings.groupby("gauge_id").size()
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    gauge_id
    G01    27
    G02    31
    G03    32
    G04    31
    G05    31
    dtype: int64
    ```

3. Count the *distinct* days for each gauge:

    ```python
    readings.groupby("gauge_id")["date"].nunique()
    ```

    You should see: G03 with 31 days, not 32, and G01 still with 27.

    ```text
    gauge_id
    G01    27
    G02    31
    G03    31
    G04    31
    G05    31
    Name: date, dtype: int64
    ```

4. Find any gauge and day with more than one row:

    ```python
    per_day = readings.groupby(["gauge_id", "date"]).size()
    per_day[per_day != 1]
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    gauge_id  date
    G03       2026-07-05    2
    dtype: int64
    ```

5. List the days on which G01 has no row:

    ```python
    july = pd.date_range("2026-07-01", "2026-07-31").strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
    sorted(set(july) - set(readings.loc[readings["gauge_id"] == "G01", "date"]))
    ```

    You should see: four consecutive days.

    ```text
    ['2026-07-22', '2026-07-23', '2026-07-24', '2026-07-25']
    ```

6. In a Markdown cell, note both findings and what each does to a monthly total.

    You should see: your note in the notebook, beside the evidence.

## Check it worked

The numbers reconcile: 155 expected rows, plus 1 repeated row, minus 4 missing days,
is 152, the size of the table.

## If it didn't

**Step 4 returns an empty result.** You ran it on a table from which repeated rows had
already been removed, for example after `drop_duplicates()`. Run the notebook's first
cell again to reload the file, then repeat the step.

# Reconcile row counts before and after a join

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    The code on this page was run with pandas 3.1 on a laptop. Nobody has yet followed
    the tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so output may be laid out differently there.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

A join can silently add rows, when a key repeats in the table you look things up in,
or lose them, when a key has no match. Counting rows before and after catches both.

**You will:** have each reading joined to its gauge's name and unit, with row counts
that prove the join changed nothing else.

**Time:** 5 to 10 minutes. **You need:** the notebook from
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/), open in
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with its first cell run so that `readings`
and `gauges` exist.

## Steps

1. Record the size of the table you are starting from:

    ```python
    len(readings)
    ```

    You should see: `152`.

2. Confirm that the lookup table has one row for each key:

    ```python
    gauges["gauge_id"].is_unique
    ```

    You should see: `True`. If a gauge appeared twice, every one of its readings would
    be doubled by the join.

3. Join, and have pandas enforce what you just checked:

    ```python
    joined = readings.merge(gauges, on="gauge_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
    ```

    You should see: no output and no error. `how="left"` keeps every reading, whether
    or not it finds a gauge.

4. Compare the sizes:

    ```python
    len(readings), len(joined)
    ```

    You should see:

    ```text
    (152, 152)
    ```

5. Count the readings that found no gauge:

    ```python
    joined["name"].isna().sum()
    ```

    You should see: `0`. Depending on the pandas version, it may be wrapped as
    `np.int64(0)`.

6. Look at the result:

    ```python
    joined.head(3)
    ```

    You should see: the four original columns, then the gauge's columns.

    ```text
      gauge_id        date  value flag       name unit  elevation_m
    0      G01  2026-07-01    0.0  NaN  Boathouse   mm          512
    1      G01  2026-07-02    0.0  NaN  Boathouse   mm          512
    2      G01  2026-07-03   24.9  NaN  Boathouse   mm          512
    ```

## Check it worked

Three numbers agree: 152 rows before, 152 rows after, and 0 readings without a match.
Each reading now carries its `unit`, which you need before values from different
gauges can be compared.

## If it didn't

**`MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a many-to-one merge`.**
The lookup table has a repeated `gauge_id`, and `validate` stopped the join before it
could multiply rows. Find the repeats with
`gauges[gauges["gauge_id"].duplicated(keep=False)]` and settle which row is right
before you join.

## Next

- [Leave a notebook someone else can rerun](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/leave-a-rerunnable-notebook/)
- A join carries problems along with it: rows repeated in `readings` are still
  repeated in `joined`. See
  [Count records per day to find incomplete days](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/count-records-per-day/).
- Reference: [pandas.DataFrame.merge](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.merge.html).

*Not yet validated in MESA JupyterLab. Drafted 2026-11-12; the code was run with pandas 3.1 on the practice data.*

# Leave a notebook someone else can rerun

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    Nobody has yet followed this tutorial in MESA JupyterLab, so a menu name may differ
    there. [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

A notebook remembers every cell you ran, in the order you ran it, including cells you
have since changed or deleted. What it shows can therefore differ from what it
produces when someone else runs it from the top.

**You will:** have a notebook that runs from a fresh start, top to bottom, without you.

**Time:** 5 to 10 minutes. **You need:** `practice.ipynb` from
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/), open in
[MESA JupyterLab](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/launch-jupyterlab/), with whatever you have added to it since.

## Steps

1. Choose **Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells…** and confirm with **Restart**.

    You should see: every code cell numbered in order down the page, `[1]`, `[2]`,
    `[3]`, with no red error box. If a cell fails, go to "If it didn't" below, then come
    back.

2. Choose **Edit → Find…** and search the notebook for `/home/`.

    You should see: no matches. A path that starts at your own home folder works only
    for you; a bare file name such as `"readings.csv"` works for anyone who has the
    file beside the notebook.

3. Click the first cell, press ++esc++, then ++a++ to add a cell above it, then ++m++
   to make it a Markdown cell. Write what the notebook does, which files it needs, and
   where they come from:

    ```markdown
    # Checks on the practice rain-gauge data

    Needs `gauges.csv` and `readings.csv` in the same folder as this notebook.
    Both are at https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/
    ```

    You should see: the heading and the text, rendered, after you press
    ++shift+enter++.

4. Add a code cell at the very end that records what the notebook ran on:

    ```python
    import sys

    print("Python", sys.version.split()[0], "| pandas", pd.__version__)
    ```

    You should see: one line with two version numbers.

5. Repeat step 1, then choose **File → Save Notebook**.

    You should see: the cells numbered in order again, and the outputs now saved in
    the file are the ones a fresh run produces.

6. Look at the `mesa-practice` folder in the file browser.

    You should see: `practice.ipynb`, `gauges.csv`, and `readings.csv`. The folder holds
    everything the notebook needs, so the folder is what you share.

## Check it worked

After **Restart Kernel and Run All Cells…**, the code cells are numbered consecutively
from `[1]` and none shows an error. Numbers that skip or run out of order mean cells
were run by hand since the last restart.

## If it didn't

**A cell stops with `NameError: name '...' is not defined`.** The cell uses something
that was defined in a cell you later deleted or changed, or in a cell further down.
It worked before only because the kernel still remembered the old definition. Put the
definition in a cell above the one that failed, then repeat step 1.

## Next

- Reference: [Managing data, "Share data"](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/portal/data/#share-data),
  for giving a colleague access to the folder.
- Reference: [Notebooks](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user/notebook.html)
  in the JupyterLab documentation.

*Not yet validated in MESA JupyterLab. Drafted 2026-11-12; the version cell was run with pandas 3.1.*

# Contribute a tutorial

The tutorials live as Markdown files in the
[idss-mesa/trainings](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings) repository[^repo]. Anyone
who can write Markdown can improve them.

## Report a problem

If a step did not match what you saw, [open an issue](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues)
with the tutorial's title, the step number, what the page said, and what you saw instead.
A screenshot helps. Leave passwords, tokens, and private data out of it.

## Fix or write a tutorial

1. Fork the repository, or create a branch if you are a member of the organization.
2. For a new tutorial, copy the [tutorial template](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/template/) into
   `docs/tutorials/<task-name>.md` and follow its rules. One task per tutorial, up to
   about 600 words.
3. Add the page in two places: the `nav` list in `zensical.toml`, and a bullet in
   `docs/tutorials/index.md` whose description matches the page's `description`.
4. Add a dated entry to `docs/log.md`.
5. Check it locally:

    ```bash
    pip install zensical pyyaml
    python scripts/okf_validate.py docs      # front matter is complete
    python scripts/gen_llms_txt.py           # regenerate llms.txt and llms-full.txt
    zensical build --clean --strict          # the site builds with no broken links
    zensical serve                           # preview at http://localhost:8000
    ```

6. Commit the regenerated `docs/llms.txt` and `docs/llms-full.txt` with your change, and
   open a pull request. Changes reach the site only through a reviewed pull request.

## What belongs here

Only what a participant or a MESA user should read.

- **Yes:** single-task tutorials, and pages that help readers find and use them.
- **No:** answer keys, facilitator notes, session plans, review checklists, or
  correspondence with partners. Those are kept elsewhere.
- **No:** features that the public [MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/)
  does not describe. Document the feature there first, then write the tutorial.
- **Never:** usernames, passwords, tokens, or keys, including in screenshots.

## Validate a tutorial

A tutorial is a draft until someone other than its author has followed it from start to
finish on the live portal. To validate one:

1. Follow every step exactly as written, in a fresh browser session.
2. At each step, compare what you see with "You should see". Note every difference,
   however small: a button with another name, a screen in another order.
3. Do the check at the end, and try the "If it didn't" slip on purpose to confirm its
   symptom and its fix.
4. Open a pull request that corrects the text and replaces the last line with the date,
   your name, and what you tested against (portal, app, and image or version).

A maintainer then removes the draft notice, sets `status: stable`, and records the
validation. Only a human maintainer adds the `verified:` key.

## License of contributions

By contributing you agree that your text and images are released under
[CC BY 4.0](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/about/license/) and any code under the BSD 3-Clause license, the same
terms as the rest of the site.

[^repo]: https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/idss-mesa/trainings repository, <https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings>.

# Tutorial template

A MESA tutorial, called a *byte*, is one short page that gets a reader through one task.
The format is modelled on UNM CARC's QuickBytes[^quickbytes], and the front matter is
the one the MESA documentation uses for every page[^docs-agents].

Copy the block below into a new file under `docs/tutorials/`, named for the task in
lower case with hyphens (`share-a-folder.md`), and replace everything in angle brackets.
[Contribute a tutorial](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/contributing/) explains the rest.

## The template

````markdown
---
type: Guide
title: "<Verb-first task, as the index will list it>"
description: "<One sentence: what the reader will have done.>"
tags: [byte, <pathway point p1-p5>, <feature>]
status: draft
generated: { by: "<human:id, or tool/version>", at: "<YYYY-MM-DD>T00:00:00Z" }
stale_after: "<review date, six months out>T00:00:00Z"
sources:
  - id: docs
    resource: "<URL of the MESA documentation page this draws on>"
    title: "<its title>"
    author: "team:idss-mesa"
---

# <Verb-first task>

!!! warning "Draft: not yet validated"
    This tutorial was written from the MESA documentation. Nobody has yet followed it
    from start to finish on the live portal, so a screen name or a step may differ.
    [Tell us what you find](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/issues).

**You will:** <one sentence naming the thing you end up with>.

**Time:** <5-10> minutes. **You need:** <account, app, or earlier tutorial, each linked>.

## Steps

1. <One action. **Screen labels** in bold.>

    You should see: <what tells you it worked>.

2. <...>

    You should see: <...>.

## Check it worked

<The one observable result that means success.>

## If it didn't

**<Symptom, as the reader sees it>.** <The single most likely cause and its fix.>

## Next

- <The tutorial that follows, linked>
- Reference: <the MESA documentation page for the full picture, linked>

*Not yet validated on the live portal. Drafted <YYYY-MM-DD> from <source>.*
````

## Rules

1. **One task, named by its verb.** "Launch JupyterLab with your Data Store mounted",
   not "JupyterLab". If the title needs "and" to join two tasks, write two tutorials.
2. **Short.** Up to about 600 words and seven steps; five to ten minutes for someone
   doing it for the first time.
3. **Six fixed parts, in this order:** what you will have, what you need, the steps, how
   to check it worked, what to do if it did not, and where to go next.
4. **Every step says what you should see.** A step without a visible result cannot be
   validated.
5. **One check at the end** that tells success from failure without judgment: a file
   listed, a count, a name on screen.
6. **One "If it didn't":** the single most likely slip, described by its symptom. If you
   need more than one, the tutorial covers too much.
7. **Link, don't repeat.** Name the MESA documentation page the tutorial draws on, and
   the tutorials before and after it. Reuse the documentation's screenshots by linking
   to them; a screenshot supports a step and never replaces it, and always has a text
   description.
8. **Names as the screen shows them, in bold.** Anything the reader types goes in a code
   block that can be copied.
9. **No credentials, ever.** Use a placeholder and one line on where readers get their
   own.
10. **Stands on its own.** A tutorial never assumes a training session, a group, or a
    schedule.
11. **Data is public, synthetic, or authorized,** with its attribution line when a
    tutorial uses a dataset.

## Front matter

| Field | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| `type` | `Guide` for a tutorial |
| `title`, `description` | The task, verb first, and one plain sentence. The description becomes the entry in the tutorial list and in `llms.txt`. |
| `tags` | Always `byte`, then one pathway tag (`p1` orient and navigate, `p2` run and understand, `p3` query and connect, `p4` explore and verify, `p5` preserve and share), then the feature |
| `status` | `draft` until someone other than the author has followed the tutorial from start to finish on the live platform, then `stable` |
| `generated` | Who or what wrote it and when: `human:<id>` for a person, `<tool>/<version>` for an AI agent or tool |
| `stale_after` | The review date, six months out. A portal or app release that changes a named screen brings it forward. |
| `sources` | The documentation pages the tutorial draws on |

There is deliberately no `verified:` key in the template. Only a human maintainer adds
it, after validation.

## The draft notice and the validation line

A tutorial that has not been validated carries the **Draft: not yet validated** notice
under its title and ends with the *Not yet validated* line. When it has been validated,
the maintainer removes the notice, sets `status: stable`, and replaces the last line
with:

```markdown
*Validated <date> by <who> on <portal, app, and image or version>.*
```

A data tutorial, one that teaches a technique on the
[practice data](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/practice-data/), words both a little differently, because
its code can be run before anyone tries it in a MESA app. Its notice says where the
code was run, and its last line reads *Not yet validated in MESA JupyterLab*. Copy
both from an existing data tutorial such as
[Load a file from your Data Store into a notebook](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/load-a-file/).

[^quickbytes]: https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/UNM CARC QuickBytes, <https://github.com/UNM-CARC/QuickBytes>.
[^docs-agents]: https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/Agent guide, MESA documentation, <https://github.com/idss-mesa/docs/blob/main/AGENTS.md>.

# License

MESA Trainings has two licenses, one for the teaching material and one for code.

| What | License | Full text |
|---|---|---|
| Training content: the tutorials, the other pages of this site, and their images | [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)[^cc-by] | [`LICENSE`](https://github.com/idss-mesa/trainings/blob/main/LICENSE) |

Copyright © 2026 The Regents of the University of New Mexico[^repo].

## Reusing a tutorial

You may copy, share, and adapt the training content for any purpose, as long as you give
credit, link to the license, and say whether you changed anything. An attribution line
such as this is enough:

```text
"<Tutorial title>" by the MESA project (https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/),
licensed CC BY 4.0. <Adapted from the original. | Unchanged.>
```

## Material from elsewhere

Screenshots of the MESA Portal are shown from the
[MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/) and belong to that project. A
tutorial that uses a dataset carries that dataset's own attribution line.

# For AI agents

This site is published for people and for AI agents. Its source is an
[Open Knowledge Format (OKF) v0.2](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md)
knowledge bundle[^okf-spec] that follows the same conventions as the MESA
documentation[^docs-agents].

## Entry points

| What | Address |
|---|---|
| Outline of every page | [`https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/llms.txt`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/llms.txt) |
| Whole site in one file | [`https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/llms-full.txt`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/llms-full.txt) |
| Markdown twin of a page | The page address plus `index.md`, for example [`https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/sign-in/index.md`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/tutorials/sign-in/index.md) |
| Raw source on GitHub | [`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/idss-mesa/trainings/main/docs/tutorials/sign-in.md`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/idss-mesa/trainings/main/docs/tutorials/sign-in.md) |

Crawlers honour only the origin's
[`https://idss-mesa.github.io/robots.txt`](https://idss-mesa.github.io/robots.txt),
which is fully permissive.

## Trust signals

- **`status: draft`** means the tutorial was written from documentation and has not
  been followed on the live portal. Treat its screen names and steps as likely, not
  confirmed, and say so when you relay them.
- **No `verified:` key** means unverified (OKF §5.3). Only a human maintainer adds it.
- **`stale_after`** is the review date. After it, check the tutorial against the
  [MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/) before relying on it.
- Tutorials tagged `byte` are single-task pages; the `p1` to `p5` tag groups them by
  stage, from first sign-in to sharing results.

## When to read something else

These pages teach people to use the portal by hand. For how a feature works, read the
[MESA documentation](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/llms.txt). For CyVerse data
itself, connect to the MESA MCP servers and call their tools, as the
[documentation's agent guide](https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/about/ai-agents/)
explains.

[^okf-spec]: https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/about/Open Knowledge Format v0.2 specification, <https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md>.
[^docs-agents]: https://idss-mesa.github.io/trainings/about/For AI agents, MESA documentation, <https://idss-mesa.github.io/docs/about/ai-agents/>.
